Good afternoon, my name is Maya Contreras. I am currently an 11th grade student at the Early College High School for Emergency Medicine located in lower Manhattan. I’m pleased to be here today alongside my incredibly brave Teen CPR team members. We’re part of a student-led effort to educate our peers in all high schools across New York City in saving lives with CPR skills. For the past few years, we worked with American Heart Association to try to bring hands-only CPR training to every school student in New York City. Our goal is simple. We want to make sure that no one is unprepared when a cardiac emergency happens. As a team of young aspiring students, we launch out into our community teaching and everyone the life-saving skill of CPR. Just recently we were at a Gotham Park and City Hall teaching and advocating to emphasize the need for change. So, we want people to see that the life they’re most likely to save is someone they love. Without help, brain damage can start in just four to six minutes, but here’s the good news: hands-only CPR and AED can double or even triple that person’s chances of surviving. Now imagine if every New York City high school student were trained in those skills, that would be about 65,000 potential life-savers every year. That’s not just a number. This would dramatically increase the number of people in these underserved communities who could potentially step in to save a life if needed. CPR training via public schools will help access and address the current inequalities.
